U.S. cancer patients need lifesaving drugs. Some have to get them in China. (https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/10/20/us-cancer-patients-need-lifesaving-drugs-some-have-get-them-china/)
【turn1095news16】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 days ago; Some U.S. cancer patients are traveling to China to access innovative and lifesaving drugs not yet available in the United States. Debbie Doppelt, a New Yorker with a rare form of lung cancer, turned to China in early 2025 for sunvozertinib, a drug targeting her tumor’s mutation, after being ineligible for U.S. clinical trials and lacking FDA-approved options. The drug, developed by Chinese firm Dizal Pharmaceutical, was approved in China in 2023 and is set for U.S. distribution in 2027 via AstraZeneca. China has rapidly become a biotech leader, offering faster and more flexible clinical trials compared to the U.S., drawing international patients and investment. In response, the U.S. launched Operation TrialBlazer to streamline approvals. Some U.S. lawmakers push for curbing collaborations with Chinese biotech, while others advocate for pragmatic, global cooperation in fighting diseases. Inspired by his mother’s experience, Max Doppelt created an AI-driven platform to help patients find clinical trials. The situation highlights challenges in U.S. drug regulations and the growing prominence of China in global drug innovation, underscoring the life-or-death stakes for patients and the need for international collaboration in medical advancements.

# Paccal Vet Feline Cancer Trial

Image: Black cat with green eyes sitting outdoors with blurred greenery in the background.

### A dose-finding study for cats with solid tumors

  * Fully funded study, no cost to pet owner

  * No placebo, all cats receive active treatment

  * Paccal Vet is based on a cancer drug widely used in human medicine

RECRUITMENT COMPLETED

## Why is this study being done?

We are studying Paccal Vet as a possible new treatment option for cats with solid tumors.

Paccal Vet is a chemotherapy that has been specifically designed for pets, and it is based on a cancer drug that is widely used and approved in human cancer care.

Several clinical trials have been performed with Paccal Vet in dogs with promising results, but to date, no studies have evaluated Paccal Vet in cats.

Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/)
【turn1095news18】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.
Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says
Date: Sat May 30 09:00:00 2026 UTC

Louise van der Weyden is a dog person. But as a scientist who studies cancer in animals, she has turned her attention to cats in recent years.
Insight into feline cancers has been like "a black box," van der Weyden said, because scientists have known so little about them.
But what she recently found after years of research surprised her: Cat cancers are similar to some human cancers, giving her hope for future advancement in treatments.
"It's a unique opportunity to help two species in one go," van der Weyden said.
The finding came from a study in which van der Weyden and other scientists across the world investigated cancer-causing genes in tumor samples of nearly 500 domestic cats - specifically which genes were commonly mutated.
The most striking similarity was in a gene called FBXW7, a critical tumor suppressor for people and cats. In cats, the gene was frequently altered in mammary tumors. Mutations in the gene are also associated with worse outcomes for people who have breast cancer.
Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa.
A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people.
For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. 
They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed.

【turn1095news19】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; The University of Queensland (UQ) Gatton has launched a clinical trial testing a new cancer drug, Enzistat, developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune. Led by Professor Rachel Allavena, the trial explores Enzistat’s potential to help dogs with inoperable or terminal tumors. Early data indicate the drug may extend survival and reduce side effects in canine cancer patients. The study is now seeking 60 participating dogs: 30 with inoperable tumours and 30 in palliative care. The goal is to shrink tumors for potential surgery or improve quality of life for terminal cases. Participants must have a cancer diagnosis and veterinary referral, and owners are required to administer the medication twice daily for six weeks and attend three visits to UQ Gatton. While the drug and necessary diagnostics are provided, all other vet costs are the owner’s responsibility. This research also holds promise for human cancer treatments. Interested parties can contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au for more information.

Of course the ChatGPT dog cancer vaccine spawned a startup (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/978671/ai-cured-dog-cancer-mrna-vaccine-startup-gamgee)
【turn1095news20】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 months ago; Paul Conyngham, an Australian tech entrepreneur, has launched a startup named Gamgee that aims to develop personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs, inspired by his own dog Rosie’s battle with cancer. He claims to have used AI tools like ChatGPT and computational genomics to craft a vaccine that led to shrinkage in Rosie's tumors. Though Gamgee focuses on pet care, its broader ambition extends to personalized treatment for various species, including humans.

Rosie’s case, which features prominently in Gamgee’s marketing, has drawn skepticism from experts who question the scientific validity of the claims, noting that Rosie received multiple treatments, making it unclear if the mRNA vaccine caused her improvement. Despite scientific uncertainties, Gamgee has received backing from Y Combinator and is preparing for clinical trials in Australia, with global recruitment underway. The company promises a simple, quick process for veterinarians and highlights promising initial results, though based on a single case.

Gamgee is collaborating with Australian universities and aims to scale its personalized medicine approach, although its foundation rests on unverified anecdotal outcomes.

This Blood Test Detects Cancer in Dogs. But Do You Want to Know? (https://www.wired.com/story/this-blood-test-detects-cancer-in-dogs-but-do-you-want-to-know)
【turn1095news21】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4.5 years ago; A new blood test called OncoK9, developed by the startup PetDx, shows promising results for cancer detection in dogs. Marketed primarily for older or high-risk dogs, the test uses liquid biopsy technology—similar to methods used in humans—to detect multiple types of cancer from cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in blood samples. In a trial involving 1,100 dogs, the test detected 85% of aggressive cancers, though its overall accuracy was a more modest 55%. The test is safer and less invasive than surgical diagnostics and can potentially buy time for palliative care or early treatment.

However, experts caution against widespread use due to ethical concerns, cost implications, and risk of false positives (around 1.5%). Some are wary of overreliance on a test that isn’t fully transparent about its algorithms and may not significantly improve outcomes without accompanying treatments. A new longitudinal study of over 1,000 dogs is now underway to evaluate its potential for early detection over time. While support and commercial backing from Petco grows, many veterinarians, including bioethicists, stress the need for careful application. For pet owners like Marina Inserra, the test gave time and clarity to make informed decisions for her dog Cici, diagnosed early with terminal hemangiosarcoma.

Your Next Dog May Live Longer (https://www.theatlantic.com/science/2026/05/celine-halioua-loyal-pet-longevity/687005/?utm_source=apple_news)
【turn1095news22】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 5 months ago; Celine Halioua, the 31-year-old founder of Loyal, a biotech company focused on canine longevity, has developed a pill that could extend dogs' lives by addressing insulin sensitivity. Approved as “likely effective” by the FDA in early 2025, Loyal's pill represents a shift toward treating aging itself rather than just organ-specific diseases. The pill, designed to boost insulin response and combat age-related diseases like cancer and heart decline, is expected to cost around $100/month and may reach the market soon, pending full regulatory approval.

Driven by her personal attachment to animals and her professional background in genetics and longevity research, Halioua chose to start with dogs for both scientific and emotional reasons. Dogs age similarly to humans, making them useful models for potential human applications. Her company has launched a five-year clinical trial involving 1,300 dogs to validate the pill's efficacy.

The broader implications of dog life-extension include potential shifts in human-animal relationships and ethical questions about affordability and euthanasia. Loyal’s success could eventually pave the way for similar treatments in human longevity. Halioua hopes to use the profits from the drug to fund future human aging research without relying on large pharmaceutical companies.

【turn1095search23】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last month; 
Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response
Medical intervention

Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response
Specialty | Oncology
Autologous patient-specific tumor antigen response (apSTAR) technology is a new cancer treatment procedure being developed by IMULAN BioTherapeutics, LLC and Veterinary Cancer Therapeutics, LLC for comparative oncology.

Also known as laser-assisted immunotherapy, apSTAR is an experimental cancer treatment for solid tumors that uses an autologous vaccine-like approach to stimulate immune responses. Specifically, laser-assisted immunotherapy combines laser-induced in situ tumor devitalization with an immunoadjuvant for local immunostimulation.
## Principles of apSTAR

The two principles underlying apSTAR are: local destruction of tumor by means of a laser combined with a photo-absorbing dye and stimulated immune response due to the application of an immunoadjuvant, but also due to increases in antigen accessibility caused by the destruction of the tumor. Both elements of this protocol are crucial. Since this method independently triggers the immune response in each individual, it does not depend upon cross reactivity in the expression of tumor-specific antigen between hosts (as is required in conventional antibody immunotherapy and vaccination.)
## Trials

Veterinary Cancer Therapeutics, LLC, a subsidiary of IMULAN BioTherapeutics, LLC, is in exploratory trials for canine osteosarcoma, canine melanoma, canine and feline fibrosarcoma, and several other forms of cancer.

A better solution? Human cancer treatment used to eliminate sarcoids in horses (https://www.horseandhound.co.uk//horse-care/histotripsy-horses-sarcoids)
【turn1095news24】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 3 weeks ago; A groundbreaking treatment for equine sarcoids, the most common and challenging skin tumors in horses, is being tested using histotripsy—a technology originally developed for human cancer treatment. Researchers at the Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine have adapted this non-invasive method that employs focused ultrasound waves to generate microscopic bubbles, shattering tumor tissues without the need for surgery or chemotherapy. A collaborative effort between engineers and veterinarians has led to the development of a wearable device capable of delivering the therapy to standing, sedated horses. The technique was successfully tested on a nine-year-old Hanoverian mare named Pea, marking the first live equine trial. The procedure was quick, without complications, and confirmed tumor destruction, although further research is needed to determine the long-term effectiveness. Dr. Sophie Bogers, leading the veterinary component, emphasized the importance of early, accessible treatment to prevent the distressing progression of sarcoids. The team is now seeking more equine participants for the trial, with hopes of developing a portable device that vets can use promptly upon sarcoid detection.

Pan-tumor CAnine cuTaneous Cancer Histology (CATCH) dataset (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11446)
【turn1095academia29】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 4.7 years ago; 
Title: Pan-tumor CAnine cuTaneous Cancer Histology (CATCH) dataset
Authors: Frauke Wilm, Marco Fragoso, Christian Marzahl, Jingna Qiu, Chloé Puget, Laura Diehl, Christof A. Bertram, Robert Klopfleisch, Andreas Maier, Katharina Breininger, Marc Aubreville
Date: Thu Jan 27 11:16:26 2022

Due to morphological similarities, the differentiation of histologic sections of cutaneous tumors into individual subtypes can be challenging. Recently, deep learning-based approaches have proven their potential for supporting pathologists in this regard. However, many of these supervised algorithms require a large amount of annotated data for robust development. We present a publicly available dataset of 350 whole slide images of seven different canine cutaneous tumors complemented by 12,424 polygon annotations for 13 histologic classes, including seven cutaneous tumor subtypes. In inter-rater experiments, we show a high consistency of the provided labels, especially for tumor annotations. We further validate the dataset by training a deep neural network for the task of tissue segmentation and tumor subtype classification. We achieve a class-averaged Jaccard coefficient of 0.7047, and 0.9044 for tumor in particular. For classification, we achieve a slide-level accuracy of 0.9857. Since canine cutaneous tumors possess various histologic homologies to human tumors the added value of this dataset is not limited to veterinary pathology but extends to more general fields of application.

Canine Olfactory Differentiation of Cancer: A Review of the Literature (https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.05495)
【turn1095academia31】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 11.1 years ago; 
Title: Canine Olfactory Differentiation of Cancer: A Review of the Literature
Authors: Oliver Gould, Amy Smart, Norman Ratcliffe, Ben de Lacy Costello
Date: Mon Oct  5 15:32:06 2015

Numerous studies have attempted to demonstrate the olfactory ability of canines to detect several common cancer types from human bodily fluids, breath and tissue. Canines have been reported to detect bladder cancer (sensitivity of 0.63-0.73 and specificity of 0.64-0.92) and prostate cancer (sensitivity of 0.91-0.99 and specificity of 0.91-0.97) from urine; breast cancer (sensitivity of 0.88 and specificity of 0.98) and lung cancer (sensitivity 0.56-0.99 and specificity of 8.30-0.99) on breath and colorectal cancer from stools (sensitivity of 0.91-0.97 and specificity of 0.97-0.99). The quoted figures of sensitivity and specificity across differing studies demonstrate that in many cases results are variable from study to study; this raises questions about the reproducibility of methodology and study design which we have identified herein. Furthermore in some studies the controls used have resulted in differentiation of samples which are of limited use for clinical diagnosis. These studies provide some evidence that cancer gives rise to different volatile organic compounds (VOCs) compared to healthy samples. Whilst canine detection may be unsuitable for clinical implementation they can, at least, provide inspiration for more traditional laboratory investigations.

PetQA: Benchmarking Veterinary Knowledge and Clinical Reasoning (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04598)
【turn1095academia32】 [wordlim: 200] Published: last month; 
Title: PetQA: Benchmarking Veterinary Knowledge and Clinical Reasoning
Authors: Taegyun Kim, Youngwook Ham, Jungwook Rhim, Ju-Hyun An, Sungkyu Park, Kunwoo Park
Date: Fri Sep  4 00:54:04 2026

We introduce PetQA, a Korean long-form question-answering (QA) benchmark for evaluating veterinary knowledge and clinical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (LVLMs). PetQA contains 10,076 text-only and 8,751 multimodal QA pairs derived from real-world questions about dogs and cats, paired with answers from expert veterinarians. Its test split, PetQA-Bench, further includes annotations for question types and clinical conditions. We evaluate eighteen models using ROUGE, BERTScore, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics for factuality and helpfulness under three settings: zero-shot inference, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The benchmarking results provide an overview of the strengths and limitations of current models in addressing veterinary clinical queries and highlight the need for more effective adaptation methods to develop clinically reliable AI systems for veterinary care. To facilitate broader use, we additionally provide translated versions of PetQA-Bench in five languages.

A completely annotated whole slide image dataset of canine breast cancer to aid human breast cancer research (https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.10244)
【turn1095academia33】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6.2 years ago; 
Title: A completely annotated whole slide image dataset of canine breast cancer to aid human breast cancer research
Authors: Marc Aubreville, Christof A. Bertram, Taryn A. Donovan, Christian Marzahl, Andreas Maier, Robert Klopfleisch
Date: Mon Aug 24 08:06:55 2020

Canine mammary carcinoma (CMC) has been used as a model to investigate the pathogenesis of human breast cancer and the same grading scheme is commonly used to assess tumor malignancy in both. One key component of this grading scheme is the density of mitotic figures (MF). Current publicly available datasets on human breast cancer only provide annotations for small subsets of whole slide images (WSIs). We present a novel dataset of 21 WSIs of CMC completely annotated for MF. For this, a pathologist screened all WSIs for potential MF and structures with a similar appearance. A second expert blindly assigned labels, and for non-matching labels, a third expert assigned the final labels. Additionally, we used machine learning to identify previously undetected MF. Finally, we performed representation learning and two-dimensional projection to further increase the consistency of the annotations. Our dataset consists of 13,907 MF and 36,379 hard negatives. We achieved a mean F1-score of 0.791 on the test set and of up to 0.696 on a human breast cancer dataset.
